desc:
Fill a grid with rows rows and cols columns using digits from 1 to 9, where no digit may be used more than once in the whole grid. Row i must add up to rowSums[i] and column j must add up to colSums[j].

Return the number of different grids that satisfy all sums (two grids differ if some cell holds different digits).

rows = 2, cols = 2, rowSums = [3, 7], colSums = [4, 6]  →  1   ([[1,2],[3,4]])
rows = 3, cols = 3, all six sums 15                      →  72  (magic squares are 8 of these)
hints: At most 9 cells are filled and each uses a distinct digit, so a search cell by cell is affordable. Write it first, then prune.
Keep the remaining sum of each row and each column. A digit is allowed in a cell only if it is unused and not larger than both the remaining row sum and the remaining column sum.

The last cell of a row has no freedom: the digit must equal the remaining row sum. The same holds for the last cell of a column. Use these forced values to cut branches, and also skip a digit that would leave a remaining sum of 0 while cells are still left in that line.
editorial: Go through the cells in row-major order and keep a bitmask of used digits plus the remaining sum of every row and column. For a cell, try each unused digit that does not exceed its row's and column's remaining sums. After the placement subtract the digit from both sums and recurse.

Two kinds of pruning shrink the tree enormously. In the last column of a row the digit is forced to be exactly the remaining row sum; in the last row it is forced to be the remaining column sum. And a digit that would bring a remaining sum to 0 while more cells of that line are still empty can never work because every digit is at least 1. For a 3 × 3 grid only the top-left 2 × 2 block is really free (at most 9 · 8 · 7 · 6 choices), the other cells are decided by the sums.
